The preference given to one or the other class of actions must necessarily be like the preference given to one or other part of the soul and its actions over the other. There must be war for the sake of peace, business for the sake of leisure, things useful and necessary for the sake of things honourable. All these points the statesman should keep in view when he frames his laws. He should consider the parts of the soul and their functions, and above all the better and the end; he should also remember the diversities of human lives and actions. Men must engage in business and go to war, but leisure and peace are better; they must do what is necessary and useful, but what is honourable is better. In such principles, children and persons of every age which requires education should be trained. Whereas even the Hellenes of the present day, who are reputed to be best governed, and the legislators who gave them their constitutions, do not appear to have framed their governments with regard to the best end, or to have given them laws and education with a view to all the virtues; but in a vulgar spirit have fallen back on those which promised to be more useful and profitable. Many modern writers have taken a similar view: they commend the Lacedaemonian constitution, and praise the legislator for making conquest and war his sole aim — a doctrine which may be refuted by argument and has long ago been refuted by facts. Most men desire empire in the hope of accumulating the goods of fortune; and on this ground Thibron and all those who have written about the Lacedaemonian constitution have praised their legislator, since the Lacedaemonians, by a training in hardships, gained great power. But surely they are not a happy people now that their empire has passed away, nor was their legislator right. How ridiculous is the result if, while they continue in the observances of his laws, and no one interferes with them, they have lost the better part of life. These writers further err about the sort of government which the legislator should approve. The government of freemen is noble, and implies more virtue than despotic government. Neither is a city to be deemed happy, nor a legislator to be praised, because he trains his citizens to conquer and obtain dominion over their neighbours, since there is great evil in this. On a similar principle, any citizen who could would obviously try to obtain the power in his own state — the crime which the Lacedaemonians accused king Pausanias of attempting, although he had so great honour already. No such principle, and no law having this object, is either statesmanlike, useful, or right. The same things are best both for individuals and for states, and these are the things which the legislator ought to implant in the minds of his citizens. Neither should men study war with a view to the enslavement of those who do not deserve to be enslaved; first of all they should provide against their own enslavement; in the second place obtain empire for the good of the governed, and not for the sake of exercising a general despotism; and in the third place, they should seek to be masters only over those who deserve to be slaves. Facts, as well as arguments, prove that the legislator should direct all his military and other measures to the provision of leisure and the establishment of peace. Most of these military states are safe only while they are at war, but fall when they have acquired their empire — like unused iron, they lose their edge in time of peace. For this the legislator is to blame, having never taught them how to lead the life of peace.

7.58.oldText: Since the end of individuals and of states is the same, the end of the best man and of the best state must also be the same. It is therefore evident that there ought to exist in both of them the virtues of leisure; for peace, as has been often repeated, is the end of war, and leisure of toil. Leisure and cultivation may be promoted not only by those virtues which are practised in leisure, but also by some of those which are useful to business — since many necessaries of life have to be supplied before we can have leisure. A city must therefore be temperate and brave, and able to endure: for truly, as the proverb says, ‘There is no leisure for slaves,’ and those who cannot face danger like men are the slaves of any invader. Courage and endurance are required for business, intellectual virtue for leisure, temperance and justice for both — more especially in times of peace and leisure, since war compels men to be just and temperate, whereas the enjoyment of good fortune and the leisure which comes with peace tends to make them insolent. Those, then, who seem to be the best off, and to be in possession of every good, have special need of justice and temperance — for example, those (if such there be, as the poets say) who dwell in the Islands of the Blest. They above all will need philosophy, temperance, and justice, and all the more the more leisure they have, living in the midst of abundance. There is no difficulty in seeing why the state that would be happy and good ought to have these virtues. If it is disgraceful in men not to be able to use the goods of life, it is peculiarly disgraceful not to be able to use them in time of peace — to show excellent qualities in action and war, and when they have peace and leisure, to be no better than slaves.

7.59.oldText: We should not, therefore, practise virtue after the manner of the Lacedaemonians. They, while agreeing with other men in their conception of the highest goods, differ from the rest of mankind in thinking that these goods are to be obtained by the practice of a single virtue. Since these goods, and the enjoyment of them, are clearly greater than the enjoyment derived from the virtues of which they are the end, we must now consider how, and by what means, they are to be attained.

7.60.oldText: We have already determined that nature, habit, and reason are required, and we have also defined what should be the character of the citizens. But we still have to consider whether the training of early life is to be that of reason or of habit, since these two must accord, and when in accord they will then form the best of harmonies. Reason may make mistakes and fail in attaining the highest ideal of life, and there may be a like evil influence of habit. Thus much is clear in the first place: as in all other things, generation starts from a beginning, and the ends of some beginnings are related to another end. In men, reason and mind are the end towards which nature strives, so that the generation and moral discipline of the citizens ought to be ordered with a view to them. In the second place, as the soul and body are two, we see also that there are two parts of the soul — the rational and the irrational — and two corresponding states: reason and appetite. As the body is prior in order of generation to the soul, so the irrational is prior to the rational.

7.61.oldText: The proof is that anger, will, and desire are implanted in children from their very birth, but reason and understanding are developed as they grow older. Hence the care of the body ought to precede that of the soul, and the training of the appetitive part should follow — none the less, our care of it must be for the sake of the reason, and our care of the body for the sake of the soul.

7.62.oldText: Since the legislator should begin by considering how the frames of the children whom he is rearing may be as good as possible, his first care will be about marriage — at what age should his citizens marry, and who are fit to marry? In legislating on this subject, he ought to consider the persons and their relative ages, that there may be no disproportion in them, and that they may not differ in their bodily powers (as will be the case if the man is still able to beget children while the woman is unable to bear them, or the woman able to bear while the man is unable to beget); from these causes arise quarrels and differences between married persons. Secondly, he must consider the time at which the children will succeed to their parents. There ought not to be too great an interval of age, since then the parents will be too old to derive any pleasure from their affection, or to be of any use to them. Nor ought they to be too nearly of an age — to youthful marriages there are many objections: the children will be wanting in respect to their parents, who will seem to be their contemporaries, and disputes will arise in the management of the household. Thirdly, and this is the point from which we digressed, the legislator must mould to his will the frames of newly-born children. Almost all these objects may be secured by attention to one point. Since the time of generation is commonly limited within the age of seventy years in the case of a man, and of fifty in the case of a woman, the commencement of the union should conform to these periods. The union of male and female when too young is bad for the procreation of children. In all other animals the offspring of the young are small and ill-developed, and generally of the female sex; the same is true of man, as is proved by the fact that in those cities in which men and women are accustomed to marry young, the people are small and weak. In childbirth, also, younger women suffer more, and more of them die. Some persons say this was the meaning of the response once given to the Troezenians — ‘Shear not the young field’ — the oracle really meant that many died because they married too young; it had nothing to do with the ingathering of the harvest. It also conduces to temperance not to marry too soon: women who marry early are apt to be wanton, and in men too the bodily frame is stunted if they marry while they are growing (since there is a time when the growth of the body ceases). Women should marry when they are about eighteen years of age, and men at thirty-seven; then they are in the prime of life, and the decline in the powers of both will coincide. Further, the children, if their birth takes place at the time which may reasonably be expected, will succeed in their prime, when the fathers are already in the decline of life, and have nearly reached their term of three-score years and ten.

7.63.oldText: Thus much of the age proper for marriage. The season of the year should also be considered. According to our present custom, people generally limit marriage to the season of winter, and they are right. The precepts of physicians and natural philosophers about generation should also be studied by the

7.64.oldText: parents themselves. The physicians give good advice about the right age of the body, and the natural philosophers about the winds — of which they prefer the north to the south.

7.65.oldText: What constitution in the parent is most advantageous to the offspring is a subject which we will hereafter consider, when we speak of the education of children; we will only make a few general remarks at present. The temperament of an athlete is not suited to the life of a citizen, or to health, or to the procreation of children, any more than the valetudinarian or exhausted constitution; but one which is in a mean between them. A man’s constitution should be inured to labour, but not to labour which is excessive, or of one sort only, such as is practised by athletes; he should be capable of all the actions of a freeman. These remarks apply equally to both parents. Women who are with child should be careful of themselves; they should take exercise and have a nourishing diet. The first of these prescriptions the legislator will easily carry into effect by requiring that they shall take a walk daily to some temple, where they can worship the gods who preside over birth. Their minds, however, unlike their bodies, they ought to keep unexercised — since the offspring derive their natures from their mothers as plants do from the earth.

7.66.oldText: As to the exposure and rearing of children, let there be a law that no deformed child shall live; but where there are too many (since in our state population has a limit), when couples have children in excess, and the state of feeling is averse to the exposure of offspring, let abortion be procured before sense and life have begun. What may or may not be lawfully done in these cases depends on the question of life and sensation.

7.67.oldText: Now, having determined at what ages men and women are to begin their union, let us also determine how long they shall continue to beget and bear offspring for the state. Men who are too old, like men who are too young, produce children who are defective in body and mind; the children of very old men are weakly. The limit, then, should be the age which is the prime of their intelligence; and this, in most persons, according to the notion of some poets who measure life by periods of seven years, is about fifty. At four or five years later, they should cease from having families; and from that time forward only cohabit with one another for the sake of health, or for some similar reason.

7.68.oldText: As to adultery, let it be held disgraceful for any man or woman to be unfaithful when they are married, and called husband and wife. If during the time of bearing children anything of the sort occur, let the guilty person be punished with a loss of privileges in proportion to the offence.

7.69.oldText: After the children have been born, the manner of rearing them may be supposed to have a great effect on their bodily strength. It would appear, from the example of animals and of those nations who desire to create the military habit, that the food which has most milk in it is best suited to human beings — but the less wine the better, if they would escape disease.

7.70.oldText: Also, all the motions to which children can be subjected at their early age are very useful. But in order to preserve their tender limbs from distortion, some nations have had recourse to mechanical appliances which straighten their bodies. To accustom children to the cold from their earliest years is also an excellent practice, which greatly conduces to health, and hardens them for military service. Hence many barbarians have a custom of plunging their children at birth into a cold stream; others, like the Celts, clothe them in a light wrapper only. Human nature should be early habituated to endure all which by habit it can be made to endure — but the process must be gradual. Children, from their natural warmth, may be easily trained to bear cold. Such care should attend them in the first stage of life.

7.71.oldText: The next period lasts to the age of five. During this, no demand should be made upon the child for study or labour, lest its growth be impeded; and there should be sufficient motion to prevent the limbs from being inactive. This can be secured, among other ways, by amusement; but the amusement should not be vulgar, tiring, or riotous. The Directors of Education, as they are termed, should be careful what tales or stories the children hear, since the sports of children are designed to prepare the way for the business of later life, and should be for the most part imitations of the occupations which they will hereafter pursue in earnest. Those are wrong who, like Plato in the Laws, attempt to check the loud crying and screaming of children, since these contribute towards their growth, and, in a manner, exercise their bodies. Straining the voice has an effect similar to that produced by the retention of the breath in violent exertions. Besides other duties, the Directors of Education should have an eye to their bringing up, and should take care that they are left as little as possible with slaves. Until they are seven years old they must live at home; and so, even at this early age, all that is mean and low should be banished from their sight and hearing. Indeed, there is nothing which the legislator should be more careful to

7.72.oldText: drive away than indecency of speech, since the light utterance of shameful words is akin to shameful actions. The young especially should never be allowed to repeat or hear anything of the sort. A freeman who is found saying or doing what is forbidden, if he be too young as yet to have the privilege of a place at the public table, should be disgraced and beaten, and an elder person degraded as his slavish conduct deserves. Since we do not allow improper language, clearly we should also banish pictures or tales which are indecent. Let the rulers take care that there be no image or picture representing unseemly actions, except in the temples of those gods at whose festivals the law permits even ribaldry, and whom the law also permits to be worshipped by persons of mature age on behalf of themselves, their children, and their wives. But the legislator should not allow youth to be hearers of satirical iambic verses or spectators of comedy until they are of an age to sit at the public tables and to drink strong wine; by that time education will have armed them against the evil influences of such representations.

7.73.oldText: We have made these remarks in a cursory manner — they are enough for the present occasion; but hereafter we will return to the subject and after a fuller discussion determine whether such liberty should or should not be granted, and in what way granted, if at all. Theodorus, the tragic actor, was quite right in saying that he would not allow any other actor, not even if he were quite second-rate, to enter before himself, since the spectators grew fond of the voices which they first heard. The same principle of association applies universally to things as well as persons — we always like best whatever comes first. Hence youth should be kept strangers to all that is bad, and especially to things which suggest vice or hate. When the five years have passed away, during the two following years they must look on at the pursuits which they are hereafter to learn. There are two periods of life into which education has to be divided: from seven to the age of puberty, and onwards to the age of twenty-one. The poets who divide ages by sevens are not always right; we should rather adhere to the divisions actually made by nature, since the deficiencies of nature are what art and education seek to fill up.

7.74.oldText: Let us, then, first inquire if any regulations are to be laid down about children; secondly, whether the care of them should be the concern of the state or of private individuals (which latter is in our own day the common custom); and in the third place, what these regulations should be.

8.0.oldText: No one will doubt that the legislator should direct his attention above all to the education of youth, or that the neglect of education does harm to states. The citizen should be moulded to suit the form of government under which he lives. Each government has a peculiar character which originally formed it, and which continues to preserve it. The character of democracy creates democracy, and the character of oligarchy creates oligarchy; and always, the better the character, the better the government.

8.1.oldText: For the exercise of any faculty or art, a previous training and habituation are required; and clearly, therefore, for the practice of virtue. Since the whole city has one end, it is manifest that education should be one and the same for all, and that it should be public, and not private — not as at present, when everyone looks after his own children separately, and gives them separate instruction of the sort which he thinks best. The training in things which are of common interest should be the same for all. Neither must we suppose that any one of the citizens belongs to himself, since they all belong to the state, and are each of them a part of the state, and the care of each part is inseparable from the care of the whole. In this particular, the Lacedaemonians are to be praised, since they take the greatest pains about their children, and make education the business of the state.

8.2.oldText: That education should be regulated by law and should be an affair of state is not to be denied — but what should be the character of this public education, and how young persons should be educated, are questions which remain to be considered. Mankind are by no means agreed about the things to be taught, whether we look to virtue or the best life. Neither is it clear whether education is more concerned with intellectual or with moral virtue. The existing practice is perplexing: no one knows on what principle we should proceed. Should the useful in life, or virtue, or higher knowledge, be the aim of our training? All three opinions have been entertained. Again, about the means there is no agreement, since different persons, starting with different ideas about the nature of virtue, naturally disagree about the practice of it. There can be no doubt that children should be taught those useful things which are really necessary, but not all things — since occupations are divided into liberal and illiberal, and to young children should be imparted only such kinds of knowledge as will be useful to them without vulgarizing them. Any occupation, art, or science which makes the body, soul, or mind of the freeman less fit for the practice or exercise of virtue is vulgar. Hence we call those arts vulgar which tend to deform the body, and likewise all paid employments — since they absorb and degrade the mind. There are also some liberal arts quite proper for a freeman to acquire, but only in a certain degree, and if he attend to them too closely, in order to attain perfection in them, the same evil effects will follow. The object also which a man sets before him makes a great difference: if he does or learns anything for his own sake, or for the sake of his friends, or with a view to excellence, the action will not appear illiberal; but if done for the sake of others, the very same action will be thought menial and servile. The received subjects of instruction, as I have already remarked, are partly of a liberal and partly of an illiberal character. The customary branches of education are four in number: (1) reading and writing, (2) gymnastic exercises, (3) music, to which is sometimes added (4) drawing. Of these, reading and writing and drawing are regarded as useful for the purposes of life in a variety of ways, and gymnastic exercises are thought to infuse courage. Concerning music a doubt may be raised — in our own day most men cultivate it for the sake of pleasure, but originally it was included in education, since nature herself, as has been often said, requires that we should be able not only to work well, but to use leisure well. As I must repeat once and again, the first principle of all action is leisure. Both are required, but leisure is better than occupation; so the question must be asked in good earnest: what ought we to do when at leisure? Clearly we ought not to be amusing ourselves — for then amusement would be the end of life. But if this is inconceivable, and yet amid serious occupations amusement is needed more than at other times (since he who is hard at work has need of relaxation, and amusement gives relaxation, whereas occupation is always accompanied with exertion and effort), at suitable times we should introduce amusements, and they should be our medicines, since the emotion which they create in the soul is a relaxation, and from the pleasure we obtain rest. Leisure of itself gives pleasure, happiness, and enjoyment of life, which are experienced not by the busy man, but by those who have leisure. He who is occupied has in view some end which he has not attained; but happiness is an end which all men deem to be accompanied with pleasure and not with pain. This pleasure, however, is regarded differently by different persons, and varies according to the habit of individuals; the pleasure of the best man is the best, and springs from the noblest sources. It is clear, then, that there are branches of learning and education which we must study with a view to the enjoyment of leisure, and these are to be valued for their own sake; whereas those kinds of knowledge which are useful in business are to be deemed necessary, and exist for the sake of other things. Hence our fathers admitted music into education, not on the ground either of its necessity or utility — since it is not necessary, nor indeed useful in the same manner as reading and writing, which are useful in money-making, in the management of a household, in the acquisition of knowledge, and in political life; nor like drawing, useful for a more correct judgment of the works of artists; nor again like gymnastic, which gives health and strength, since neither of these is to be gained from music. There remains, then, the use of music for intellectual enjoyment in leisure, which appears to have been the reason of its introduction — this being one of the ways in which it is thought that a freeman should pass his leisure. As Homer says,

8.3.oldText: ‘How good is it to invite men to the pleasant feast,’ and afterwards he speaks of others whom he describes as inviting ‘the bard who would delight them all.’

8.4.oldText: And in another place Odysseus says there is no better way of passing life than when ‘men’s hearts are merry, and the banqueters in the hall, sitting in order, hear the voice of the minstrel.’ It is evident, then, that there is a sort of education in which parents should train their sons, not as being useful or necessary, but because it is liberal or noble. Whether this is of one kind only, or of more than one, and if so, what they are, and how they are to be imparted, must hereafter be determined. Thus much we are now in a position to say: that the ancients witness to us, since their opinion may be gathered from the fact that music is one of the received and traditional branches of education. Further, it is clear that children should be instructed in some useful things — for example, in reading and writing — not only for their usefulness, but also because many other sorts of knowledge are acquired through them. With a like view they may be taught drawing — not to prevent their making mistakes in their own purchases, or in order that they may not be imposed upon in the buying or selling of articles, but rather because it makes them judges of the beauty of the human form. To be always seeking after the useful does not become free and exalted souls. Now it is clear that in education, habit must go before reason, and the body before the mind; and so boys should be handed over to the trainer, who creates in them the proper habit of body, and to the wrestling-master, who teaches them their exercises.

8.5.oldText: Of those states which in our own day seem to take the greatest care of children, some aim at producing in them an athletic habit, but they only injure their forms and stunt their growth.

8.6.oldText: Although the Lacedaemonians have not fallen into this mistake, yet they brutalize their children by laborious exercises which they think will make them courageous. But in truth, as we have often repeated, education should not be exclusively directed to this or to any other single end. Even if we suppose the Lacedaemonians to be right in their end, they do not attain it. Among barbarians and among animals, courage is found associated, not with the greatest ferocity, but with a gentle and lion-like temper. There are many races who are ready enough to kill and eat men — such as the

8.7.oldText: Achaeans and Heniochi, who both live about the Black Sea; and there are other inland tribes, as bad or worse, who all live by plunder, but have no courage. It is notorious that the Lacedaemonians, while they were themselves assiduous in their laborious drill, were superior to others, but now they are beaten both in war and in gymnastic exercises. Their ancient superiority did not depend on their mode of training their youth, but only on the circumstance that they trained them at a time when others did not. Hence we may infer that what is noble, not what is brutal, should have the first place — no wolf or other wild animal will face a really noble danger; such dangers are for the brave man. Parents who devote their children to gymnastics while they neglect their necessary education, in reality vulgarize them; for they make them useful to the state in one quality only, and even in this the argument proves them to be inferior to others. We should judge the Lacedaemonians not from what they have been, but from what they are; for now they have rivals who compete with their education, whereas formerly they had none.

8.8.oldText: It is an admitted principle that gymnastic exercises should be employed in education, and that for children they should be of a lighter kind, avoiding severe regimen or painful toil, lest the growth of the body be impaired. The evil of excessive training in early years is strikingly proved by the example of the Olympic victors: not more than two or three of them have gained a prize both as boys and as men, since their early training and severe gymnastic exercises exhausted their constitutions. When boyhood is over, three years should be spent in other studies; the period of life which follows may then be devoted to hard exercise and strict regimen. Men ought not to labour at the same time with their minds and with their bodies, since the two kinds of labour are opposed to one another — the labour of the body impedes the mind, and the labour of the mind the body.

8.9.oldText: Concerning music there are some questions which we have already raised; these we may now resume and carry further. Our remarks will serve as a prelude to this or any other discussion of the subject. It is not easy to determine the nature of music, or why anyone should have a knowledge of it. Shall we say, for the sake of amusement and relaxation, like sleep or drinking, which are not good in themselves, but are pleasant, and at the same time ‘make care to cease,’ as Euripides says? And so men rank them with music, and make use of all three — sleep, drinking, music — to which some add dancing. Or shall we argue that music conduces to virtue, on the ground that it can form our minds and habituate us to true pleasures, as our bodies are made by

8.10.oldText: gymnastic to be of a certain character? Or shall we say that it contributes to the enjoyment of leisure and mental cultivation, which is a third alternative? Now obviously youth are not to be instructed with a view to their amusement, since learning is no pleasure, but is accompanied with pain. Neither is intellectual enjoyment suitable to boys of that age, since it is the end, and that which is imperfect cannot attain the perfect or the end. But perhaps it may be said that boys learn music for the sake of the amusement which they will have when they are grown up. If so, why should they learn themselves, and not, like the Persian and Median kings, enjoy the pleasure and instruction which is derived from hearing others — since surely skilled persons who have made music the business and profession of their lives will be better performers than those who practise only to learn? If they must learn music, on the same principle they should learn cookery, which is absurd. Even granting that music may form the character, the objection still holds: why should we learn ourselves? Why cannot we attain true pleasure and form a correct judgment from hearing others, like the Lacedaemonians? — for they, without learning music, can nevertheless correctly judge, as they say, of good and bad melodies. Or again, if music should be used to promote cheerfulness and refined intellectual enjoyment, the objection still remains: why should we learn ourselves instead of enjoying the performances of others? We may illustrate what we are saying by our conception of the gods: in the poets, Zeus does not himself sing or play on the lyre. Indeed, we call professional performers vulgar; no freeman would play or sing unless he were intoxicated or in jest. But these matters may be left for the present.

8.11.oldText: The first question is whether music is or is not to be a part of education. Of the three things mentioned in our discussion, which is it? Education, amusement, or intellectual enjoyment? It may be reckoned under all three, and seems to share in the nature of all of them. Amusement is for the sake of relaxation, and relaxation is of necessity sweet, since it is the remedy of pain caused by toil; and intellectual enjoyment is universally acknowledged to contain an element not only of the noble but of the pleasant, since happiness is made up of both. All men agree that music is one of the pleasantest things, whether with or without song. As Musaeus says,

8.12.oldText: ‘Song is to mortals of all things the sweetest.’ Hence, with good reason, it is introduced into social gatherings and entertainments, since it makes the hearts of men glad. So on this ground alone we may assume that the young ought to be trained in it. Innocent pleasures are not only in harmony with the perfect end of life, but they also provide relaxation. And whereas men rarely attain the end, but often rest by the way and amuse themselves, not only with a view to some good but also for the pleasure’s sake, it may be well for them at times to find a refreshment in music.

8.13.oldText: It sometimes happens that men make amusement the end, since the end probably contains some element of pleasure — though not any ordinary or lower pleasure. They mistake the lower for the higher, and in seeking for the one find the other, since every pleasure has a likeness to the end of action. The end is not eligible for the sake of any future good but of the past, that is, these pleasures are the alleviation of past toils and pains. We may infer this to be the reason why men seek happiness from common pleasures.

8.14.oldText: But music is pursued not only as an alleviation of past toil, but also as providing recreation. Who can say whether, having this use, it may not also have a nobler one? In addition to this common pleasure, felt and shared in by all (since the pleasure given by music is natural, and therefore adapted to all ages and characters), may it not have also some influence over the character and the soul? It must have such an influence if characters are affected by it. That they are so affected is proved by the power which the songs of Olympus and of many others exercise; for beyond question they inspire enthusiasm, and enthusiasm is an emotion of the ethical part of the soul. Besides, when men hear imitations, even unaccompanied by melody or rhythm, their feelings move in sympathy. Since, then, music is a pleasure, and virtue consists in rejoicing and loving and hating aright, there is clearly nothing which we are so much concerned to acquire and to cultivate as the power of forming right judgments, and of taking delight in good dispositions and noble actions. Rhythm and melody supply imitations of anger and gentleness, and also of courage, temperance, and of virtues and vices in general — imitations which hardly fall short of the actual affections, as we know from our own experience: in listening to such strains, our souls undergo a change. The habit of feeling pleasure or pain at mere representations is not far removed from the same feeling about realities. If anyone delights in the sight of a statue for its beauty only, it necessarily follows that the sight of

8.15.oldText: the original will be pleasant to him. No other sense, such as taste or touch, has any resemblance to moral qualities; in sight only there is a little, since figures are to some extent of a moral character, and so far all participate in the feeling about them. Again, figures and colours are not imitations, but signs of moral habits, and these signs occur only when the body is under the influence of emotions. The connection of them with morals is slight; but in so far as there is any, young men should be taught to look, not at the works of Pauson, but at those of Polygnotus or any other painter or statuary who expresses moral ideas. On the other hand, even in mere melodies there is an imitation of character, since the musical modes differ essentially from one another, and those who hear them are differently affected by each. Some of them make men sad and grave, like the so-called Mixolydian; others enfeeble the mind, like the relaxed harmonies; others again produce a moderate and settled temper, which appears to be the peculiar effect of the Dorian; the Phrygian inspires enthusiasm. The whole subject has been well treated by philosophical writers on this branch of education, and they confirm their arguments by facts. The same principles apply to rhythms: some have a character of rest, others of motion; and of these latter, some have a more vulgar, others a nobler movement. Enough has been said to show that music has a power of forming the character, and should therefore be introduced into the education of the young. The study is suited to the stage of youth, since young persons will not, if they can help it, endure anything which is not sweetened by pleasure, and music has a natural sweetness. There seems to be in us a sort of affinity to harmonies and rhythms, which makes some philosophers say that the soul is a harmony, others that she possesses harmony.

8.16.oldText: And now we have to determine the question which has been already raised: whether children should be themselves taught to sing and play, or not. Clearly there is a considerable difference made in the character by the actual practice of the art. It is difficult, if not impossible, for those who do not perform to be good judges of the performance of others. Besides, children should have something to do, and the rattle of Archytas, which people give to their children in order to amuse them and prevent them from breaking anything in the house, was a capital invention — since a young thing cannot be quiet. The rattle is a toy suited to the infant mind, and musical education is a rattle or toy for children of a larger growth. We conclude, then, that they should be taught music in such a way as to become not only critics but performers.

8.17.oldText: The question what is or is not suitable for different ages may be easily answered; nor is there any difficulty in meeting the objection of those who say that the study of music is vulgar. We reply (1) in the first place, that they who are to be judges must also be performers, and that they should begin to practise early, although when they are older they may be spared the execution; they must have learned to appreciate what is good and to delight in it, thanks to the knowledge which they acquired in their youth. As to (2) the vulgarizing effect which music is supposed to exercise, this is a question of degree, which we shall have no difficulty in determining, when we have considered to what extent freemen who are being trained to political virtue should pursue the art, what melodies and what rhythms they should be allowed to use, and what instruments should be employed in teaching them to play — since even the instrument makes a difference. The answer to the objection turns upon these distinctions, since it is quite possible that certain methods of teaching and learning music do really have a degrading effect. It is evident, then, that the learning of music ought not to impede the business of riper years, or to degrade the body or render it unfit for civil or military duties, whether for the early practice or for the later study of them.

8.18.oldText: The right measure will be attained if students of music stop short of the arts which are practised in professional contests, and do not seek to acquire those fantastic marvels of execution which are now the fashion in such contests, and from these have passed into education. Let the young pursue their studies until they are able to feel delight in noble melodies and rhythms, and not merely in that common part of music in which every slave or child, and even some animals, find pleasure.

8.19.oldText: From these principles we may also infer what instruments should be used. The flute, or any other instrument which requires great skill — such as the harp — ought not to be admitted into education, but only such as will make intelligent students of music or of the other parts of education. Besides, the flute is not an instrument which has a good moral effect; it is too exciting. The proper time for using it is when the performance aims not at instruction, but at the relief of the passions. There is a further objection: the impediment which the flute presents to the use of the voice detracts from its educational value. The ancients, therefore, were right in forbidding the flute to youths and freemen, although they had once allowed it. When their wealth gave them greater leisure, and they had loftier notions of excellence, being also elated with their success both before and after the Persian War, with more zeal than discernment they pursued every kind of knowledge, and so they introduced the flute into education. At Lacedaemon there was a Choragus who led the chorus with a flute, and at Athens the instrument became so popular that most freemen could play upon it. The popularity is shown by the tablet which Thrasippus dedicated when he furnished the chorus to Ecphantides. Later experience enabled men to judge what was, or what was not, really conducive to virtue, and they rejected both the flute and several other old-fashioned instruments, such as the Lydian harp, the many-stringed lyre, the ‘heptagon,’ ‘triangle,’ ‘sambuca,’ and the like, which are intended only to give pleasure to the hearer, and require extraordinary skill of hand. There is a meaning also in the myth of the ancients, which tells how Athene invented the flute and then threw it away. It was not a bad idea of theirs, that the goddess disliked the instrument because it made the face ugly; but with still more reason may we say that she rejected it because the acquirement of flute-playing contributes nothing to the mind, since to Athene we ascribe knowledge and art.

8.20.oldText: Accordingly, we reject the professional instruments and also the professional mode of education in music — and by professional we mean that which is adopted in contests, since in this the performer practises the art, not for the sake of his own improvement, but in order to give pleasure, and that of a vulgar sort, to his hearers. For this reason, the execution of such

8.21.oldText: music is not the part of a freeman, but of a paid performer; and the result is that the performers are vulgarized, since the end at which they aim is bad. The vulgarity of the spectator tends to lower the character of the music, and therefore of the performers; they look to him — he makes them what they are, and fashions even their bodies by the movements which he expects them to exhibit. We have also to consider rhythms and harmonies. Shall we use them all in education, or make a distinction? And shall the distinction be that which is made by those who are engaged in education, or shall it be some other? We see that music is produced by melody and rhythm, and we ought to know what influence these have respectively on education, and whether we should prefer excellence in melody or excellence in rhythm. But as the subject has been very well treated by many musicians of the present day, and also by philosophers who have had considerable experience of musical education, to these we would refer the more exact student of the subject; we shall only speak of it now after the manner of the legislator, having regard to general principles.

8.22.oldText: We accept the division of melodies proposed by certain philosophers into ethical melodies, melodies of action, and passionate or inspiring melodies, each having, as they say, a mode or harmony corresponding to it. But we maintain further that music should be studied, not for the sake of one, but of many benefits — that is, with a view to (1) education, (2) purgation (the word ‘purgation’ we use at present without explanation, but when hereafter we speak of poetry, we will treat the subject with more precision); music may also serve (3) for intellectual enjoyment, for relaxation, and for recreation after exertion. It is clear, therefore, that all the harmonies must be employed by us, but not all of them in the same manner. In education, ethical melodies are to be preferred; but we may listen to the melodies of action and passion when they are performed by others. For feelings such as pity and fear, or, again, enthusiasm, exist very strongly in some souls, and have more or less influence over all. Some persons fall into a religious frenzy, whom we see disenthralled by the use of mystic melodies — which bring healing and purgation to the soul. Those who are influenced by pity or fear, and every emotional nature, have a like experience; others in their degree are stirred by something which specially affects them, and all are in a manner purged, and their souls lightened and delighted. The melodies of purgation likewise give an innocent pleasure to mankind. Such are the harmonies and the melodies in which those who perform music at the theatre should be invited to compete. But since the spectators are of two kinds — the one free and educated, the other a vulgar crowd composed of mechanics, labourers, and the like — there ought to be contests and exhibitions instituted for the relaxation of the second class also. The melodies will correspond to their minds: as their minds are perverted from the natural state, so there are exaggerated and corrupted harmonies which are in like manner a perversion. A man receives pleasure from what is natural to him, and so professional musicians may be allowed to practise this lower sort of music before an audience of a lower type. But for the purpose of education, as I have already said, those modes and melodies should be employed which are ethical, such as the Dorian — though we may include any others which are approved by philosophers who have had a musical education. The Socrates of the

8.23.oldText: Republic is wrong in retaining only the Phrygian mode along with the Dorian, and the more so because he rejects the flute. The Phrygian is to the modes what the flute is to musical instruments — both of them are exciting and emotional.

8.24.oldText: Poetry proves this, since Bacchic frenzy and all similar emotions are most suitably expressed by the flute, and are better set to the Phrygian than to any other harmony. The dithyramb, for example, is acknowledged to be Phrygian — a fact of which the connoisseurs of music offer many proofs, saying, among other things, that Philoxenus, having attempted to compose his Tales as a dithyramb in the Dorian mode, found it impossible, and fell back into the more appropriate Phrygian. All men agree that the Dorian music is the gravest and manliest. Whereas we say that the extremes should be avoided and the mean followed, and whereas the Dorian is a mean between the other harmonies (the Phrygian and the Lydian), it is evident that our youth should be taught the Dorian music.

8.25.oldText: Two principles have to be kept in view: what is possible, and what is becoming. At these every man ought to aim. But even these are relative to age. The old, who have lost their powers, cannot very well sing the severe melodies, and nature herself seems to suggest that their songs should be of the more relaxed kind. Hence the musicians likewise blame Socrates, and with justice, for rejecting the relaxed harmonies in education under the idea that they are intoxicating — not in the ordinary sense of intoxication (since wine rather tends to excite men), but because they have no strength in them. With a view, then, to a time of life when men begin to grow old, they ought to practise the gentler harmonies and melodies as well as the others. And if there is any harmony — such as the Lydian above all others appears to be — which is suited to children of tender age, and possesses the elements both of order and of education, we ought to use it. Education should be based upon three principles: the mean, the possible, and the becoming, these three.

1.1.oldText: Der findes en fejlagtig opfattelse, hvorefter statsmanden, kongen, husstandens overhoved og slaveherren alle er det samme og kun adskiller sig fra hinanden ved antallet af dem, de hersker over, ikke ved arten af deres herredømme. Ifølge denne opfattelse kaldes den, der hersker over få, en herre; den, der hersker over flere, en husholder; og den, der hersker over endnu flere, en statsmand eller konge — som om der ikke var nogen reel forskel på en stor husstand og en lille stat. Den formodede forskel mellem konge og statsmand skulle være denne: når herredømmet er personligt, kaldes herskeren konge; når borgerne efter den politiske videnskabs principper hersker og bliver hersket på skift, kaldes han statsmand.

1.2.oldText: Men alt dette er en fejltagelse, for styreformer er forskellige i art. Det vil stå klart for enhver, der følger den metode, vi hidtil har anvendt. Som i andre grene af forskningen, sådan også i politik: det sammensatte må altid opløses i sine simpleste elementer eller mindste dele. Vi må derfor se på de elementer, der udgør staten, for at se, hvordan de adskiller sig fra hinanden, og om der kan trækkes nogen videnskabelig skelnen mellem de forskellige former for herredømme.

1.3.oldText: Den, der betragter tingene i deres første vækst og oprindelse — uanset om det er en stat eller noget andet — vil få det klareste billede af dem. For det første må der være en forening af dem, der ikke kan eksistere uden hinanden. Der er foreningen mellem mand og kvinde, så slægten kan fortsætte. Denne forening dannes ikke ud fra bevidst hensigt, men fordi mennesker, ligesom andre dyr og planter, har et naturligt ønske om at efterlade et billede af sig selv. Der må også være en forening mellem den naturlige hersker og den underordnede, så begge kan bevares. For den, der kan se forud med sin forstand, er af naturen bestemt til at være herre og mester, mens den, der kan arbejde med sin krop, er underordnet og af naturen slave; derfor har herre og slave samme interesse. Naturen har imidlertid skelnet mellem kvinden og slaven. Hun er ikke nærig som smeden, der laver den delfiske kniv til mange formål; hun skaber hver ting til ét enkelt formål, og ethvert redskab er bedst lavet, når det er beregnet til én anvendelse og ikke til mange. Blandt barbarerne gøres der dog ingen forskel mellem kvinder og slaver, fordi der ikke findes nogen naturlig hersker iblandt dem: de er et fællesskab af slaver, mandlige og kvindelige. Derfor siger digterne —

1.4.oldText: »Det sømmer sig, at hellenere hersker over barbarer« — som om de mente, at barbaren og slaven af naturen var ét og det samme.

1.6.oldText: »Først et hus, og en hustru, og en okse til ploven« — for oksen er den fattige mands slave. Familien er den sammenslutning, naturen har oprettet til at dække menneskenes daglige behov. Dens medlemmer kaldes af Charondas »skabsfæller« [omosipuous] og af Epimenides fra Kreta »krybbefæller« [omokapous]. Men når flere familier forenes, og sammenslutningen sigter mod noget mere end den daglige forsyning, opstår landsbyen. Den mest naturlige form for landsby synes at være en koloni fra familien, bestående af børn og børnebørn, som siges at være »diet med samme mælk«. Det er grunden til, at hellenske stater oprindelig blev styret af konger: hellenerne var under kongeligt styre, før de slog sig sammen, ligesom barbarerne stadig er. Enhver familie styres af den ældste, og således herskede den kongelige styreform også i koloniudgaverne af familien, eftersom de var af samme blod. Som Homer siger om kykloperne:

1.9.oldText: Når flere landsbyer forenes i ét enkelt fællesskab, der er fuldstændigt og stort nok til næsten eller helt at være selvtilstrækkeligt, opstår staten. Den udspringer af livets bare nødvendigheder, men den fortsætter med at eksistere for det gode livs skyld. Og hvis altså de tidligere samfundsformer er naturlige, så er staten det også, for den er deres mål, og den fuldendte natur er målet. Hvad enhver ting er, når den er fuldt udviklet, kalder vi dens natur, hvad enten vi taler om et menneske, en hest eller en familie. Desuden er en tings endemål og fuldbyrdelse det bedste, og selvtilstrækkelighed er målet og det bedste.

1.10.oldText: Det er derfor klart, at staten er en skabelse af naturen, og at mennesket af natur er et politisk dyr. Den, der af natur og ikke ved en tilfældighed er uden stat, er enten over menneskeligheden eller under den. Han er den

1.13.oldText: Således er staten af natur klart forud for familien og for individet, eftersom helheden nødvendigvis er forud for delen. Hvis hele kroppen ødelægges, vil der ikke være nogen fod eller hånd undtagen i en tvetydig betydning — som vi kunne tale om en stenhånd; for når den først er ødelagt, vil hånden ikke være bedre end den. Ting defineres ved deres funktion og evne, og vi bør ikke sige, at de er de samme, når de ikke længere er de samme, men kun at de deler det samme navn. Beviset for, at staten er en skabelse af naturen og forud for individet, er, at individet, når det er isoleret, ikke er selvtilstrækkeligt og derfor er som en del i forhold til helheden. Den, der ikke er i stand til at leve i samfundet, eller som ikke har behov for det, fordi han er sig selv nok, må enten være et dyr eller en gud — han er ikke en del af en stat. Et socialt instinkt er nedlagt i alle mennesker af naturen, og dog var den, der først grundlagde staten, den største af velgørere. For mennesket er, når det er fuldendt, det bedste af dyrene, men når det er adskilt fra lov og retfærdighed, er det det værste af alle. Bevæbnet uretfærdighed er den farligste, og mennesket er fra fødslen udstyret med intelligensens våben og med moralske egenskaber, som det kan bruge til de værste formål. Hvis det altså mangler dyd, er det det mest ugudelige og det mest vilde af alle dyr, det fyldigste af lyst og frådseri. Retfærdighed er båndet, der binder mennesker i stater, og forvaltningen af retfærdighed — afgørelsen af, hvad der er retfærdigt — er ordensprincippet i det politiske samfund.

1.17.oldText: »af sig selv trådte ind i gudernes forsamling«; eller hvis skytten på samme måde kunne væve, og plekteret kunne røre lyren uden en hånd til at føre dem — da ville mesterhåndværkere ikke have brug for tjenere, og herrer ikke for slaver. Der må dog drages endnu en sondring her: de redskaber, som almindeligvis kaldes så, er produktionsredskaber, hvorimod en besiddelse er et handlingsredskab. Skytten, for eksempel, er ikke alene til brug; der laves noget andet med den. Med en klædning eller en seng er der derimod kun brugen. Eftersom produktion og handling er forskellige i art, og begge kræver redskaber, må de redskaber, de anvender, ligeledes være forskellige i art. Men livet er handling, ikke produktion, og derfor er slaven handlingens tjener — for han tjener sin herres liv. Endvidere omtales en besiddelse på den måde, en del omtales: for en del er ikke alene en del af noget andet, men tilhører det helt og holdent; og dette gælder også for en besiddelse. Herren er kun slavens herre; han tilhører ikke ham. Slaven er derimod ikke alene sin herres slave, men tilhører ham helt og holdent. Heraf ser vi en slaves natur og embede: den, der af natur ikke er sin egen, men en andens, og dog er et menneske, er af natur en slave. Han kan siges at tilhøre en anden, som, idet han er et menneske, også er en besiddelse. En besiddelse kan defineres som et handlingsredskab, der kan adskilles fra besidderen.

1.19.oldText: Der er ingen vanskelighed ved at besvare dette spørgsmål, både ud fra fornuft og ud fra kendsgerninger. For at nogle skal herske, og andre skal være underordnede, er ikke alene nødvendigt, men også gavnligt. Lige fra fødslens stund er nogle udpeget til underkastelse, andre til herredømme.

1.20.oldText: Der findes mange slags herskere og underordnede, og det herredømme, der udøves over bedre underordnede, er selv det bedre — at herske over mennesker er for eksempel bedre end at herske over vilde dyr. Det arbejde, der udføres af bedre arbejdere, er det bedre arbejde, og hvor den ene hersker og den anden bliver hersket, kan de siges at have del i en fælles opgave. I alle ting, der udgør et sammensat hele bestående af dele — hvad enten de er sammenhængende eller adskilte — træder en sondring mellem det herskende og det underordnede element frem. En sådan dobbelthed findes hos levende væsener, men ikke kun hos dem; den udspringer af universets indretning. Selv i livløse ting findes der et herskende princip, som i den musikalske harmoni. Men vi afviger fra emnet. Lad os derfor begrænse os til det levende væsen, som først og fremmest består af sjæl og krop. Af disse to er den ene af natur hersker og den anden underordnet. Vi må imidlertid søge naturens hensigter i ting, der bevarer deres natur, ikke i ting, der er fordærvede. Vi må derfor studere det menneske, der er i den fuldkomneste tilstand både af krop og sjæl, for i ham vil vi se de tos sande forhold — selv om kroppen i dårlige eller fordærvede naturer ofte synes at herske over sjælen, fordi de befinder sig i en ond og unaturlig tilstand. For det første kan vi altså iagttage hos levende væsener både et despotisk og et forfatningsmæssigt herredømme. Sjælen hersker over kroppen med et despotisk herredømme, mens forstanden hersker over begæringerne med et forfatningsmæssigt og kongeligt herredømme. Det er klart, at sjælens herredømme over kroppen, og det rationelle elements herredømme over det lidenskabelige, er naturligt og gavnligt — hvorimod ligheden mellem de to, eller det underordnedes herredømme, altid er skadelig. Det samme gælder for dyr såvel som for mennesker. Tamme dyr har en bedre natur end vilde, og alle tamme dyr har det bedre, når de styres af mennesket, for så bliver de bevaret. Endvidere er hannen af natur overlegen, hunnen underlegen; den ene hersker, og den anden bliver hersket. Dette princip strækker sig nødvendigvis til hele menneskeheden. Hvor der findes en sådan forskel som den mellem sjæl og krop eller mellem mennesker og dyr — som hos dem, hvis hverv er at bruge deres krop, og som ikke kan udrette noget bedre — er den lavere slags af natur slaver, og det er bedre for dem, som for alle underordnede, at de er under en herres styre. For den, der kan være, og derfor er, en andens, og som har del i fornuften netop nok til at fatte den, men ikke til at besidde den, er af natur slave. De lavere dyr kan ikke engang fatte fornuften; de adlyder deres instinkter. Faktisk er den brug, der gøres af slaver og af tamme dyr, ikke meget forskellig, for begge tjener med deres kroppe livets behov. Naturen ville gerne skelne mellem frie mænds og slavers kroppe, idet den gør den ene stærk til trællearbejde, den anden rank — og selv om den er ubrugelig til en sådan tjeneste, er den nyttig i det politiske liv i krigens og fredens kunster. Men dette gælder ikke universelt: for nogle slaver har frie mænds sjæle, og andre har deres kroppe. Og hvis menneskene virkelig adskilte sig fra hinanden i deres rene legemsformer i samme grad, som gudernes statuer adskiller sig fra mennesker, ville alle erkende, at den underlegne klasse burde være slaver af den overlegne. Hvis der er en forskel i kroppen, hvor meget mere må der ikke være i sjælen? Men kroppens skønhed ses, hvorimod sjælens skønhed ikke ses. Det er altså klart, at nogle mennesker er af natur frie og andre slaver, og at slaveri for de sidstnævnte er både gavnligt og rigtigt.

1.21.oldText: Dog kan det også let ses, at de, der indtager den modsatte opfattelse, har en vis ret på deres side. Ordene »slaveri« og »slave« bruges i to betydninger. Der er en slave eller et slaveri ved lov, såvel som ved natur. Den lov, jeg taler om, er en slags overenskomst, hvorefter alt, hvad der tages i krig, tilhører sejrherrerne. Mange retslærde anfægter denne ret, sådan som de ville anfægte en taler, der foreslog en uforfatningsmæssig forholdsregel: de afskyr den tanke, at fordi én mand har magt til at udøve vold og er overlegen i rå styrke, skal en anden være hans slave og underordnede. Selv blandt filosoffer er der uenighed. Stridighedens oprindelse, og grunden til, at argumenterne krydser hinanden, er denne. Dyd, når den er udstyret med midler, kan anses for at have den største magt til at udøve vold; og eftersom overlegen magt kun findes, hvor der er overlegen fortræffelighed af én eller anden art, anses magt for at indebære dyd. Men indebærer den ligeledes retfærdighed? Det er spørgsmålet. For at trække en sondring mellem dem hævder nogle, at retfærdighed er velvilje, mens andre svarer, at retfærdighed ikke er andet end den overlegnes herredømme. Hvis de to opfattelser tages som modsatte og udelukkende — det vil sige, hvis tanken om, at retfærdighed er velvilje, udelukker tanken om en retfærdig hersken ved en overlegen — så har alternativet, nemlig at ingen bør herske over andre, ingen styrke eller plausibilitet, eftersom det indebærer, at end ikke den, der er overlegen i dyd, bør herske eller være herre. Nogle, der som de tror klamrer sig til et retfærdighedsprincip (for lov og sædvane er en slags retfærdighed), antager, at slaveri i krig retfærdiggøres ved lov — men de er ikke konsekvente. For hvad nu, hvis krigens årsag er uretfærdig? Ingen ville nogensinde sige, at en, der er uværdig til at være slave, med rette er slave. Hvis det forholdt sig sådan, ville mænd af højeste rang være slaver, og slavers børn også, hvis de eller deres forældre tilfældigvis var blevet taget til fange og solgt. Det er grunden til, at hellenere ikke kan lide at kalde sig selv for slaver, men begrænser udtrykket til barbarer. Men når de bruger dette sprog, mener de i virkeligheden den naturlige slave, vi talte om i begyndelsen; for det må indrømmes, at nogle er slaver overalt, andre ingen steder. Det samme princip gælder for adel. Hellenere anser sig selv for at være ædle overalt, ikke kun i deres eget land, men de anser kun barbarer for ædle hjemme — hvilket antyder, at der er to slags adel og frihed: den ene absolut, den anden relativ. Helena hos Theodektes siger,

1.22.oldText: »Hvem ville driste sig til at kalde mig tjener, når jeg på begge sider stammer fra gudernes stamme?«

1.23.oldText: Hvad betyder dette andet, end at de skelner frihed og slaveri, ædel og lav byrd, ud fra de to principper godt og ondt? De mener, at ligesom mennesker og dyr avler mennesker og dyr, sådan udspringer en god mand af gode mænd. Men det er, hvad naturen, selv om hun måtte tilstræbe det, ofte ikke evner at fuldbyrde.

1.24.oldText: Vi ser altså, at der er en vis grund til denne meningsforskel, og at nogle faktiske slaver og frie mænd ikke er det af natur, mens der i nogle tilfælde er en markant sondring mellem de to klasser — som gør det gavnligt og rigtigt, at den ene skal være slaver og de andre herrer: den ene udøver lydighed, den anden udøver den autoritet, som naturen havde tiltænkt dem. Misbrug af denne autoritet er skadelig for begge, for delens og helhedens, kroppens og sjælens interesser er de samme; slaven er en del af herren, en levende, men adskilt del af hans legemlige skikkelse. Hvor forholdet mellem dem er naturligt, er de venner og har en fælles interesse; hvor det kun hviler på lov og magt, er det modsatte tilfældet.

1.25.oldText: De foregående bemærkninger er ganske tilstrækkelige til at vise, at en herres herredømme ikke er et forfatningsmæssigt herredømme, og at alle de forskellige former for herredømme derfor ikke, som nogle hævder, er de samme. Der er ét herredømme, der udøves over underordnede, som af natur er frie, og et andet over underordnede, som af natur er slaver. Husstandens herredømme er et monarki, for hvert hus står under ét overhoved; hvorimod forfatningsmæssigt herredømme er styre over frie mænd og ligemænd. Herren kaldes ikke herre, fordi han har en videnskab, men fordi han er af en bestemt karakter — og det samme gælder slaven og den frie mand. Alligevel kan der være en videnskab for herren og en videnskab for slaven. Slavens videnskab ville være som den, der blev undervist af manden fra Syrakus, der tjente penge ved at undervise slaver i deres almindelige pligter. En sådan kundskab kan udvides til at omfatte madlavning og lignende ringe håndværk. Nogle pligter er af den mere nødvendige slags, andre af den mere ærefulde — som ordsproget siger: »slave før slave, herre før herre«. Men alle sådanne grene af kundskaben er trællesager. Der findes ligeledes en herrens videnskab, som lærer brugen af slaver; for herren som sådan beskæftiger sig ikke med erhvervelsen af slaver, men med deres brug. Dog er denne såkaldte videnskab ikke noget stort eller forunderligt, eftersom herren kun behøver at vide, hvordan han skal befale, hvad slaven skal vide, hvordan han skal udføre. Derfor har de, hvis stilling sætter dem over slid, godsbestyrere til at tage sig af deres husstande, mens de selv beskæftiger sig med filosofi eller med politik. Kunsten at erhverve slaver — kunsten, det vil sige, at erhverve dem retfærdigt — adskiller sig både fra herrens kunst og slavens kunst og er en form for jagt eller krig. Nok om sondringen mellem herre og slave.

1.26.oldText: Lad os nu undersøge ejendom i almindelighed og kunsten at tjene penge i overensstemmelse med vores sædvanlige metode med at opløse en helhed i sine dele — for slaven er blevet vist at være en del af ejendommen. Det første spørgsmål er, om kunsten at tjene penge er den samme som husholdning eller en del af den eller blot et redskab for den; og hvis et redskab, om det er på den måde, hvorpå kunsten at lave skytter er et redskab for vævning, eller på den måde, hvorpå støbning af bronze er et redskab for billedhuggerkunsten. For disse er ikke redskaber på samme måde: den ene leverer værktøj, den anden leverer materiale — og med materiale mener jeg det grundstof, hvoraf et hvilket som helst arbejde er fremstillet. Uld er væverens materiale, bronze er billedhuggerens. Det er let at se, at husholdning ikke er identisk med kunsten at tjene penge, for den ene bruger det materiale, den anden leverer. Den kunst, der bruger husstandens forråd, kan ikke være andet end husholdning. Der er imidlertid en vis tvivl om, hvorvidt kunsten at tjene penge er en del af husholdning eller en særskilt kunst. De synes at være forbundne, eftersom pengeskaberen må overveje, hvor penge og ejendom kan skaffes. Men der er mange slags ejendom og rigdom. Der er agerbrug og forsorg og tilvejebringelse af føde i almindelighed — er disse dele af kunsten at tjene penge eller særskilte kunster? Der er endvidere mange slags føde og derfor mange slags liv, både hos dyr og mennesker. De må alle have føde, og forskellene i deres føde har frembragt forskelle i deres levevis. Af dyr er nogle flokdyr, andre enkeltgængere; de lever på den måde, der bedst er egnet til at opretholde dem, alt efter om de er kødædende, planteædende eller altædende. Deres vaner er bestemt af naturen på en sådan måde, at de lettere kan skaffe sig den føde, de foretrækker. Men eftersom forskellige individer har forskellig smag, er de samme ting ikke af naturen behagelige for dem alle; og således adskiller selv de kødædende og de planteædende dyrs liv sig endvidere indbyrdes. Også i menneskenes liv er der stor mangfoldighed. De mest dovne er hyrder, der fører et lediggangsliv og uden besvær får deres underhold fra tamme dyr; deres flokke må vandre fra sted til sted i søgen efter græsgang, og hyrderne er nødt til at følge dem og dyrke en slags levende gård. Andre underholder sig ved jagt, som er af forskellige slags. Nogle er sørøvere; andre, der bor nær søer, sumpe, floder eller et hav, hvor der er fisk, er fiskere; andre lever af at jage fugle eller vildt. Det største antal får deres underhold fra jordens frugter. Dette er de underholdsformer, der hersker blandt dem, hvis flid er rettet direkte mod naturens frembringelser, og hvis føde ikke skaffes ved bytte eller detailhandel — der er hyrden, agerbrugeren, sørøveren, fiskeren, jægeren. Nogle får et bekvemt udkomme af to beskæftigelser kombineret og udfylder den enes mangler med den anden: en hyrdes liv kan kombineres med en røvers, en agerbrugers liv med en jægers. Andre levevis kombineres på lignende måde, alt efter hvad menneskenes behov måtte kræve. Ejendom i betydningen et bart udkomme synes at være givet af naturen selv til alle, både ved fødslen og når de er voksne. Nogle dyr bringer sammen med deres afkom føde nok til at vare, indtil de unge kan forsyne sig selv — vermipare og ovipare dyr er et eksempel — og de viviparre dyr bærer i sig selv, indtil et vist punkt, et forråd af føde til deres unge, der kaldes mælk. På samme måde kan vi slutte, at planter efter dyrenes fødsel eksisterer for dyrenes skyld, og at de øvrige dyr eksisterer for menneskets skyld — de tamme til brug og føde, de vilde, hvis ikke alle, så i hvert fald størstedelen af dem, til føde og til tilvejebringelse af klæder og forskellige redskaber. Hvis altså naturen ikke laver noget ufuldstændigt og intet forgæves, må slutningen være, at hun har skabt alle dyr og planter for menneskets skyld. Og således er krigskunsten ud fra ét synspunkt en naturlig erhvervelseskunst, for den indbefatter jagt — en kunst, vi bør udøve mod vilde dyr og mod de mennesker, der, skønt af naturen bestemt til at blive styret, ikke vil underordne sig. Krig af denne slags er naturligt retfærdig.

1.29.oldText: Men der er en grænse fastsat, ligesom der er i kunsterne: for redskaberne i ethvert håndværk er aldrig ubegrænsede i antal eller størrelse, og rigdom kan defineres som en mængde redskaber, der skal bruges i en husstand eller i en stat. Vi ser altså, at der findes en naturlig erhvervelseskunst, som udøves af husholdere og statsmænd, og vi har set grunden til den.

1.30.oldText: Der findes en anden variant af erhvervelseskunsten, som almindeligvis og med rette kaldes kunsten at tjene penge, og som faktisk har givet anledning til den forestilling, at rigdom og ejendom ingen grænse har. Da den er nært forbundet med den foregående, identificeres den ofte med den. Men selv om de ikke er meget forskellige, er de heller ikke de samme. Den allerede beskrevne form gives af naturen; den anden vindes ved erfaring og kunst.

1.32.oldText: Af alt, hvad vi besidder, er der to anvendelser, som begge tilhører tingen som sådan, men ikke på samme måde: den ene er den egentlige, den anden den uegentlige eller sekundære anvendelse. En sko bruges for eksempel til at gå med og bruges til bytte — begge er anvendelser af skoen. Den, der giver en sko i bytte for penge eller mad til en, der har brug for én, bruger ganske vist skoen som sko, men dette er ikke dens egentlige eller primære formål, for en sko er ikke lavet for at være genstand for bytte. Det samme kan siges om alle besiddelser, for byttekunsten omfatter dem alle. Den opstår først på en naturlig måde af det forhold, at nogle har for lidt og andre for meget. Heraf kan vi slutte, at detailhandel ikke er en naturlig del af kunsten at tjene penge; havde den været det, ville menneskene være holdt op med at bytte, når de havde nok. I det første fællesskab, som er familien, er denne kunst klart til ingen nytte, men begynder først at være nyttig, når samfundet vokser. Familiens medlemmer havde oprindelig alt til fælles; i en mere opdelt samfundstilstand delte de stadig meget, men havde forskellige ting at give i bytte for det, de ønskede — en form for bytte, der stadig udøves blandt barbariske folkeslag, der bytter livets fornødenheder med hinanden og intet mere, og giver og modtager for eksempel vin i bytte for korn og lignende. Denne form for bytte er ikke en del af kunsten at tjene penge og strider ikke mod naturen, men er nødvendig til tilfredsstillelse af menneskenes naturlige behov. Den anden og mere sammensatte form for bytte voksede ud af den enklere. Da indbyggerne i ét land blev mere afhængige af indbyggerne i et andet og indførte, hvad de havde brug for, og udførte deres overskud, kom penge nødvendigvis i brug. Livets forskellige fornødenheder kan ikke let bæres rundt, og således blev menneskene enige om i deres mellemværender at anvende noget, der var iboende nyttigt og let anvendeligt til livets formål — for eksempel jern, sølv og lignende. Dets værdi blev først målt ved størrelse og vægt, men med tiden satte de et stempel på det for at spare besværet med at veje og for at angive værdien.

1.33.oldText: Da brugen af mønter først var blevet opdaget, opstod af bytte med nødvendige varer den anden kunst at tjene penge — nemlig detailhandel. Dette var sandsynligvis i begyndelsen en simpel sag, men blev mere indviklet, så snart menneskene af erfaring lærte, hvorfra og ved hvilke bytter den største fortjeneste kunne opnås. Da kunsten at tjene penge har sin oprindelse i brugen af mønter, anses den almindeligvis for først og fremmest at angå dem og at være den kunst, der frembringer rigdom og penge — idet den må overveje, hvordan de kan akkumuleres. Faktisk antages rigdom af mange kun at være en mængde mønter, fordi kunsten at tjene penge og detailhandel angår mønter. Andre hævder, at mønter er et rent blændværk, en ting, der ikke er naturlig, men kun vedtægtsmæssig, og som ingen værdi eller anvendelse ville have til nogen af det daglige livs formål, hvis brugerne erstattede den med en anden vare. Og faktisk kan den, der er rig på mønter, ofte mangle nødvendig føde. Hvordan kan det være rigdom, som en mand kan have i stor overflod og dog omkomme af sult — som Midas i fablen, hvis umættelige bøn forvandlede alt, hvad der blev sat foran ham, til guld?

1.34.oldText: Mennesker søger en bedre forståelse af rigdom og af kunsten at tjene penge end den blotte erhvervelse af mønter, og de har ret til at gøre det. Naturlig rigdom og den naturlige kunst at tjene penge er noget andet; i deres sande form er de en del af husholdning. Detailhandel er derimod kunsten at frembringe rigdom — ikke på enhver måde, men ved bytte. Den synes at angå mønter, for mønter er byttets udgangspunkt og mål. Der er ingen grænse for den rigdom, der udspringer af denne kunst at tjene penge. Som der i lægekunsten ikke er nogen grænse for stræben efter sundhed, og som der i de andre kunster ikke er nogen grænse for stræben efter deres respektive mål — for de sigter mod at fuldbyrde deres mål til det yderste (skønt der er en grænse for midlerne, eftersom målet altid er grænsen) — således er der heller ingen grænse for målet i denne kunst at tjene penge, hvilket er rigdom af den uægte slags, nemlig erhvervelse af penge. Men husholdning har en grænse: den ubegrænsede erhvervelse af penge er ikke dens hverv. Og således må al rigdom set ud fra ét synspunkt have en grænse. Men i virkeligheden finder vi det modsatte at være tilfældet, for alle pengeskabere forøger deres beholdning af mønter uden grænse. Forvirringens kilde er den nære forbindelse mellem de to slags pengeskaben. I begge er redskabet — det vil sige rigdommen — det samme, selv om brugen er forskellig, og således går de over i hinanden. Hver er en brug af samme ejendom, men med en forskel: ophobning er målet i det ene tilfælde, mens der er et videre mål i det andet. Heraf ledes nogle til at tro, at det at tjene penge er husholdningens formål, og hele tanken bag deres liv er, at de enten bør forøge deres penge uden grænse eller i det mindste ikke miste dem. Denne dispositions oprindelse er, at de kun er optaget af at leve, ikke af at leve godt; og da deres begæringer er ubegrænsede, ønsker de også, at midlerne til at tilfredsstille dem skal være uden grænse. Selv de, der sigter mod et godt liv, søger midlerne til at opnå legemlige fornøjelser, og da nydelsen af disse synes at afhænge af ejendom, er de optaget af at tjene penge. Således opstår den anden art af pengeskaben. Da deres nydelse er overdreven, søger de en kunst, der frembringer overdreven nydelse; og hvis de ikke er i stand til at forsyne deres fornøjelser ved kunsten at tjene penge, prøver de andre kunster og bruger på skift hver evne på en måde, der strider mod naturen. Modets egenskab, for eksempel, er ikke beregnet til at tjene penge, men til at indgyde tillid; og dette er heller ikke målet for generalens eller lægens kunst — den ene sigter mod sejr, den anden mod sundhed. Dog forvandler nogle mennesker enhver egenskab og enhver kunst til et middel til at tjene penge. Dette opfatter de som målet, og til dets fremme må alt bidrage.

1.35.oldText: Således har vi behandlet den unødvendige kunst at tjene penge og grunden til, at menneskene ønsker den; vi har også behandlet den nødvendige kunst at tjene penge, som vi har set er forskellig fra den anden, og som er en naturlig del af husholdning, der angår tilvejebringelse af føde — dog ikke, ligesom den førstnævnte slags, ubegrænset, men med en grænse.

1.36.oldText: Og vi har fundet svaret på vores oprindelige spørgsmål, om kunsten at tjene penge er husholderens og statsmandens hverv eller ikke — nemlig at det er en kunst, som forudsættes af dem. Den politiske videnskab skaber ikke mennesker, men tager dem fra naturen og bruger dem; og naturen forsyner dem med føde fra jordens, luftens eller havets element. På dette stadium begynder husholderens pligt, der må ordne de ting, naturen leverer. Han kan sammenlignes med væveren, der ikke skal lave, men bruge uld, og som skal vide, hvilken slags uld der er god og brugbar, og hvilken slags der er dårlig og ubrugelig. Var det anderledes, ville det være vanskeligt at se, hvorfor kunsten at tjene penge er en del af husholdning, mens lægekunsten ikke er — for husstandens medlemmer må sikkert have sundhed, ligesom de må have liv eller en hvilken som helst anden fornødenhed. Ud fra ét synspunkt må husets herre og statens hersker tage hensyn til sundhed; ud fra et andet er det ikke dem, men lægen. Således må husholdning ud fra én vinkel, ud fra en anden den underordnede kunst, tage hensyn til penge. Strengt taget må livets midler dog, som jeg allerede har sagt, tilvejebringes på forhånd af naturen; for naturens hverv er at skaffe føde til det, der er født, og afkommets føde forbliver altid tilbage hos forælderen. Heraf er kunsten at tjene penge på frugter og dyr altid naturlig.

1.37.oldText: Af de to slags pengeskaben er den ene, som jeg lige har sagt, en del af husholdning, den anden er detailhandel. Den førstnævnte er nødvendig og hæderlig; den sidstnævnte er en form for bytte, der med rette dadles, for den er unaturlig og en måde, hvorpå menneskene vinder på hinandens bekostning. Den mest forhadte slags, og med størst grund, er åger, der vinder gevinst af pengene selv, ikke af deres naturlige brug. Penge var beregnet til at blive brugt til bytte, ikke til at vokse ved rente. Selve udtrykket »åger« — tokos, der betyder pengenes fødsel af penge — anvendes på pengenes formering, fordi afkommet ligner forælderen. Af alle måder at tjene penge på er denne den mest unaturlige.

1.38.oldText: Tilstrækkeligt er sagt om teorien om at tjene penge; vi vil nu vende os til den praktiske del. Behandlingen af sådanne sager er ikke filosofien uværdig, men at beskæftige sig med dem praktisk er uædelt og besværligt. De nyttige dele af pengeskaben er for det første kendskab til kvæg — hvilke slags der er mest fortjenstlige, og hvor og hvordan. For eksempel hvilken slags heste, får, okser eller andre dyr der med størst sandsynlighed giver et udbytte. En mand bør vide, hvilke af disse der betaler bedre end andre, og hvilke der betaler bedst på bestemte steder, for nogle klarer sig bedre på ét sted og andre på et andet.
